analysis.one_liner: Requires federal contractors and the federal government to pay workers a poverty-level living wage for a family of four.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 81 House cosponsors, never got a vote: it sat in two committees and their subcommittees from March 2001 until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the federal government and any company holding a federal contract over $10,000 to pay every worker enough — at 40 hours a week — to lift a family of four above the federal poverty line, plus extra pay to cover benefits like health insurance the employer did not provide. Companies that repeatedly violated it could lose their contracts and be barred from new federal work for five years. Workers could also sue for back pay and, in willful cases, triple damages. Small businesses and most nonprofits were exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage federal and federal contract workers — roughly 162,000 contract workers earned below a family-of-four poverty wage in fiscal 1999, along with over 14,000 federal employees as of September 2000, according to the bill's findings.

how_it_helps.text: The bill found that about 162,000 federal contract workers — 11 percent of the 1.4 million federal contract workforce — did not earn enough at full-time work to lift a family of four out of poverty, and that 14,356 federal employees earned below that level as of September 2000.

It required employers under contracts above $10,000 to pay a wage that, at 40 hours a week, matches the federal poverty line for a family of four, adjusted by locality to cover benefits like health insurance and retirement contributions the employer does not provide.

Contractors with a pattern of violations could have their contracts canceled and be barred from federal contracting for five years, and workers could sue for back pay, attorney fees, and triple damages in willful cases.
The bill banned employers from firing or suspending a worker for alleging a wage violation.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors — large firms in particular, since the bill's findings say just under 60 percent of the underpaid contract workers worked for large firms and 62 percent worked on Defense Department contracts — would face higher labor costs, which would flow through to the price of government work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal contractors, especially large defense firms

drawbacks.text: Contractors would bear higher labor costs on more than $208 billion in annual federal contract awards (fiscal 1999), and those costs would largely be passed on to the government — meaning taxpayers fund much of the raise.

The wage floor is set by the poverty line for a family of four, so it would pay a single worker with no dependents the same family-size-based wage — a one-size-fits-all benchmark that pays some workers more than a household-needs standard would.
The bill exempted small businesses and nonprofits whose CEO-to-lowest-worker pay ratio was 25-to-1 or less, leaving large nonprofit and small-firm employers outside the requirement entirely.

Employers would face litigation exposure through the private right of action, including treble damages for willful violations, which supporters of contractors argued raised the risk of costly disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: workers currently paid below a poverty-level family wage — disproportionately adult women and minorities, per the bill's findings — would get a substantial raise, while contractors' costs would rise and much of the increase would likely be passed through to the federal budget. The bill's carve-outs for small businesses and low-ratio nonprofits narrow both the benefit and the disruption, and its penalties are targeted at repeat violators rather than first mistakes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, sent down to subcommittees within weeks, and never moved again — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the Federal Living Wage Responsibility Act on March 7, 2001, with 62 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on Government Reform and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
By the end of April 2001 it had been sent to the Subcommittee on Technology and Procurement Policy and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; the full list of cosponsors grew to 81.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 107th Congress, which ended January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors — particularly the large firms and Defense Department contractors that employ most of the affected low-wage workers — avoided a higher wage floor and debarment penalties, while the roughly 176,000 below-poverty-wage workers the bill identified gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal contractors; low-wage workers gained nothing

against.what_they_did: Controlled the committees and floor schedule in the 107th Congress; the bill received no hearing, markup, or vote. No Republican cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All 81 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their labor costs and exposed repeat violators to contract cancellation and a five-year federal contracting ban. Its findings placed just under 60 percent of underpaid contract workers at large firms and 62 percent on Defense Department contracts.
They were exempt from the wage requirement, so they would face none of the new labor costs their larger competitors would bear.
Exempt only if their CEO earned no more than 25 times their lowest-paid full-time worker; nonprofits with wider pay gaps would have been covered.
